newsitem.title: HONG KONG: Asian Sugar - China domestic sugar price seen lower.
newsitem.headline: Asian Sugar - China domestic sugar price seen lower.

text.p: China's domestic sugar prices have dipped even lower as the crushing season runs full tilt and refineries face another year of losses, sugar industry sources in Hong Kong and China said on Wednesday.

Rumours that a cargo of sugar from Thailand and another from Australia totalling about 50,000 tonnes arrived earlier this month at one northern and one southern port had also weighed on prices, a China-based sugar trader said.

"The sugar was bought on last year's quota," the trader said, adding that the rumour was unconfirmed but was weighing on prices. Sugar traders said sugar in the southern province of Guangxi, China's prime producing area, had dropped to around 3,950 yuan ($476) per tonne from 4,000 ($482) last week.
"Refineries will make a loss," said a sugar trader in Hong Kong.
Unforthcoming government credit to pay farmers for cane and increasing coal prices had added to sugar refineries' woes, Hong Kong traders said.
Government intervention looked remote, sugar traders said.
"The government will not provide credit to loss-making enterprises," one sugar source said, noting that factories had made losses last year and were facing losses this year.

Domestic sugar price weakness would continue until the middle of February, after the Chinese New Year, but would firm if the government did not allow imports in the first half, a Beijing-based trader said.
Japanese traders said nearby premiums for Thai raw sugar would be supported because of delayed crushing in Thailand, but an influx of cheaper Cuban sugar would cap the topside.
Premiums for January/March delivery were quoted at 0.75/0.80 cents (bid/offer) per pound over New York's Coffee, Sugar and Cocoa Exchange on an FOB basis.
March/May and May/July deliveries were quoted at 0.40/0.45 cents and 0.48/0.55 cents on the New York exchange, they said.
Overall bearish premiums for Thai raw sugar remained, partly due to International Sugar Organisation (ISO) estimates about a higher sugar surplus, traders said.
A total of 28 sugar mills were now in operation, compared with 19 as of December 10, a source at the Thai industry ministry said on Tuesday.

"We were informed that Thailand's crushing this season is slightly behind schedule because rainfalls delayed collection of sugarcane," a major trade house official said. "This will help support the January/March premiums for Thai raw sugar."
But traders said cheaper Cuban sugar was expected to enter the market gradually, capping the topside of the premiums.
Japan's Nissho Iwai Corp said on Wednesday it was in the freight market for Cuban sugar for January to February shipment.
"We're in the freight market for Cuban sugar," a Nissho Iwai official said. He did not elaborate.
(US$1 = 8.3 yuan)
